model.name: AI Inference / Agent Run
model.purpose: Provide the format-neutral context structure an AI agent needs to open, execute, observe, close, audit, cost and retain a single AI inference or agent run, so that what was asked, what was configured, what was invoked, what was produced, at whose authority, at what cost and with what evidence can be reconstructed after the fact.
model.scope_statement: One bounded execution occurrence of an AI system: from the moment an invocation is accepted until the run reaches a terminal state, plus the durable record of that occurrence. The run is an occurrent (a PROV Activity) that references, but does not define, the agent that performed it, the configuration it was bound to, or the AI system it belongs to. It covers single model calls, agentic loops, orchestrated multi-agent workflows and asynchronous or batched executions whose result is retrieved later. It is storage- and interface-neutral: OTLP spans, JSON log records, Git-tracked files, MongoDB documents and MCP resources are projections of the same semantics.
in_scope: Run identity, correlation to traces, conversations and parent runs
Invocation inputs, system instructions and their trust provenance
Binding to a specific model, provider, endpoint and immutable configuration snapshot
Capability surface offered to the run (tools, resources, data sources) and its authorization scopes
Ordered step trajectory including model calls, planning steps, tool calls and delegated sub-runs
Run state machine, termination reason, error classification and partial completion
Outputs, structured results and provenance manifests attached to generated assets
Principals, on-behalf-of delegation chains and human oversight interventions
Token, resource and monetary consumption attributable to the run
Evaluation results, guardrail decisions and other quality evidence bound to the run
Statutory record-keeping, retention, legal hold, deletion, access scoping and record integrity
Export profiles and lossy-mapping declarations to external telemetry and provenance schemas
out_of_scope: Definition, capabilities, persona and lifecycle of the agent itself (WM-AI-002)
Prompt templates, parameter defaults, weights and versioned configuration content (WM-AI-005)
AI system registration, model cards, training data and conformity assessment (WM-AI-001)
Conversation, session or thread as a container entity that groups many runs
Evaluation campaign design, benchmark definition and dataset curation
Incident management, post-market monitoring cases and regulatory reporting workflows
Pricing schedules, rate cards, invoices and contractual billing terms
Person and organisation master data for users, approvers and deployers
Compute infrastructure inventory, capacity planning and rate-limit configuration
Physical actuation, robot motion planning and safety envelopes

boundary_notes.distinction: The agent is a continuant that bears responsibility; the run is the occurrence it performs. PROV-O separates prov:Agent from prov:Activity and links them with prov:wasAssociatedWith. The run stores only a reference plus the agent identity attributes observed at execution time (gen_ai.agent.id, gen_ai.agent.name); it never redefines the agent.

The run references an immutable, content-addressed configuration snapshot. Parameter semantics, defaults and version history belong to the configuration model; the run records only which snapshot was in force and any per-call overrides actually sent.

A trace is a correlation mechanism, not the run. OpenTelemetry trace-ids are 16-byte values that may be unsampled, absent, shared across many runs, or restarted at a process boundary; the run keeps trace-id and span-id as correlation keys, never as identity.

gen_ai.conversation.id groups runs that share a history; it is Conditionally Required telemetry, not run identity. A conversation container entity, if modelled, is a sibling aggregate that references runs; embeddings and classification runs have no conversation at all.

OpenTelemetry defines gen_ai.evaluation.result as a separate event that may be emitted asynchronously after the run. The run holds references to evaluation results and their verdicts; evaluator definitions, rubrics and campaign scope stay outside.

A C2PA manifest asserts provenance of an asset, not of an execution. It is attached to outputs of the run as a downstream artifact; there is no normative C2PA field that carries a run identifier, so the binding is an adopting-Dimension convention and must be recorded as such.

EU AI Act Articles 12 and 19 impose automatic-logging and retention duties on providers of high-risk AI systems. The run record is the technical substrate that can satisfy those duties, but the obligation, its addressee and its assessment belong to the AI system governance model, not to this model.

MCP defines the wire contract for tools/list and tools/call. The run records which tool was called with which arguments and what came back; tool schemas, annotations and server capabilities are external declarations that the run snapshots by reference and digest.

sources.title: W3C Trace Context, Level 1
sources.relevance: Defines the traceparent header as version-trace-id-parent-id-trace-flags with a 16-byte trace-id and 8-byte parent-id, and the tracestate vendor key/value list, establishing how runs correlate across process and vendor boundaries.

sources.title: PROV-O: The PROV Ontology
sources.relevance: Supplies the Entity/Activity/Agent split and the wasGeneratedBy, used, wasDerivedFrom, wasAttributedTo, wasAssociatedWith, actedOnBehalfOf, startedAtTime and endedAtTime properties used to type a run as an activity with attributable inputs and outputs.

sources.title: Model Context Protocol specification 2026-07-28: Authorization
sources.relevance: Requires OAuth 2.1, RFC 8707 resource indicators on every authorization and token request, audience-bound token validation, refusal to accept or transit foreign tokens, and per-operation scope challenges; supplies the authority model for what a run was permitted to do.

sources.title: RFC 3339: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps
sources.relevance: Defines the full-date and full-time grammar, mandatory numeric UTC offset or Z, optional fractional seconds, and the -00:00 convention for an unknown local offset; governs every instant recorded on a run.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), U.S. Department of Commerce
sources.version_or_date: NIST AI 100-1, released 26 January 2023; Generative AI Profile NIST AI 600-1 released 26 July 2024
sources.relevance: Voluntary framework whose GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE functions justify measurement, evidence and accountability layers over runs, and whose Generative AI Profile motivates content provenance and human-AI configuration oversight.

sources.title: Claude Messages API reference
sources.relevance: Concrete response shape for a model call: message id, content blocks including thinking and tool_use, model, stop_reason values end_turn/max_tokens/stop_sequence, stop_sequence, and usage with input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens; also marks temperature, top_p and top_k as deprecated for newer models.

sources.title: Usage and Cost API
sources.relevance: Shows authoritative usage and cost reporting as time-bucketed aggregates (1m/1h/1d) grouped by model, workspace, api_key_id, service_tier, context_window, inference_geo and speed, with costs in USD and a stated data-freshness lag; establishes that per-run cost is derived, not billed.

sources.title: Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3
sources.relevance: A concrete invocation-log record schema: schemaType, schemaVersion, timestamp, accountId, region, requestId, operation, modelId, identity.arn, caller-supplied requestMetadata, and input/output bodies with token counts, including the 100 KB inline limit above which payloads are externalised to object storage.

sources.title: C2PA Specification, version 2.2
sources.organization: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA)
sources.relevance: Defines manifest, claim, assertions, ingredients, hard binding and claim signature, and the c2pa.actions assertion with digitalSourceType values used to disclose that an asset was produced with generative AI.

bundles.name: Run identity and classification
bundles.description: What this run is, how it is named, how it is correlated to surrounding executions, and which operational and regulatory class it falls into.
bundles.rationale: Every downstream concern - provenance, cost, retention, audit - hangs off a stable run identity and a correct class. Vendors each mint their own identifier (response id, message id, requestId) and none of them is globally governed, so identity must be decided explicitly before anything else. Classification decides which obligations even apply.

layers.name: Identity and correlation
layers.description: The authoritative identifier for the run and the correlation keys that place it inside a trace, a conversation and a chain of related runs.

findings.name: Authoritative run identifier
findings.description: Which identifier authoritatively names this run, which system issued it, how it behaves under retries and asynchronous retrieval, and which vendor-native identifiers are kept alongside it. OpenTelemetry marks gen_ai.response.id as Required only for fetch_response operations, Anthropic returns a msg_ prefixed message id, and Amazon Bedrock records a requestId; none of these is a governed global identifier, so the adopting Dimension must state its priority order.

questions.text: Which system is the master of record for this run's identifier, and what is the exact literal form of that identifier?
answer_data: Name and URI of the issuing master system

questions.text: When the executing provider returns no run identifier, what identifier does the adopting Dimension mint, and how is uniqueness guaranteed?
Does the identifier stay stable across retries, streaming resumption and later asynchronous result retrieval, or does each attempt receive a new one?
Which vendor-native identifiers are retained beside the authoritative identifier, and what is each one good for?

artifacts.identity_strategy: Named by the authoritative run identifier; the record is the identity anchor for every other artifact in this model.

findings.name: Trace, conversation and parent-run correlation
findings.description: The keys that place the run inside a wider execution graph: W3C trace-id and span-id, gen_ai.conversation.id for session grouping, and the parent-run edge for delegated executions. These are correlation, not identity: trace-ids may be unsampled or absent, and a conversation groups many runs.

questions.text: Which trace identifier and span identifier bind this run into the surrounding distributed trace, and in which propagation format?
Which conversation, session or thread identifier groups this run with the runs that preceded and followed it?
How are correlation keys preserved when the run crosses a process, vendor or network boundary?
What is recorded when the trace is not sampled, telemetry is dropped, or no conversation exists for this operation type?

artifacts.description: Exported telemetry covering the run and its child spans, used to reconstruct the execution graph independently of the run record.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by trace identifier plus the root span identifier of the run; never used as the run's own identity.

layers.name: Operation typing and risk classification
layers.description: The operational shape of the run and the regulatory or risk class that determines which obligations attach to it.

findings.name: Operation type and invocation mode
findings.description: Which operation the run represents and how it was invoked. OpenTelemetry enumerates chat, embeddings, retrieval, fetch_response, create_agent, invoke_agent, invoke_workflow, plan and execute_tool; the run must also record whether execution was synchronous, streaming, batched or asynchronously retrieved, because that changes where the run's temporal boundaries lie.

questions.text: Which operation type does this run represent, drawn from a closed and versioned code list?
Was the run synchronous, streaming, batched or asynchronously retrieved, and where exactly do its temporal boundaries fall?
Does this run represent a single model call or an agentic loop that may contain many model and tool calls?

data_elements.name: Operation name
data_elements.description: Coded operation type such as chat, embeddings, invoke_agent, plan or execute_tool.

data_elements.name: Invocation mode
data_elements.description: Synchronous, streaming, batch or deferred-retrieval execution mode.

data_elements.name: Agentic loop flag
data_elements.description: Whether the run contains an iterative reason-act loop rather than one call.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Operation typing is a small set of coded scalar attributes carried on the run record declared under find-run-identifier. It produces no separate deliverable, and minting a distinct artifact would create a second, competing identity anchor for the same execution.

findings.name: Regulatory and oversight classification
findings.description: Whether the AI system executing this run falls into a regulated class, which minimum log content that triggers, and what level of human oversight is mandated. EU AI Act Article 12 obligations attach only to high-risk systems, and the Article 12(3) minimum log set applies only to Annex III point 1(a) remote biometric identification, so over-application is a real modelling error.

questions.text: Under which regulatory regime and which risk category is the AI system performing this run classified, and by whose determination?
Does the applicable regime impose a minimum log content set for runs of this class, and is every mandated element actually present?
What degree of human oversight must be exercised over runs of this class before their effects take hold?
Which jurisdictions' obligations apply to this run, given where it executed and where its effects land?

data_elements.name: Regulatory class
data_elements.description: Coded risk classification of the executing AI system under an applicable regime.

data_elements.name: Mandated log element set
data_elements.description: The minimum log elements the applicable regime requires for this run class.

data_elements.name: Required oversight level
data_elements.description: Level of human oversight mandated before the run's effects take place.

data_elements.name: Applicable jurisdictions
data_elements.description: Jurisdictions whose obligations attach to this run.

findings.inline_only_rationale: The classification is inherited from the AI system registration held in the parent model and is carried on the run only as coded references plus the determination reference. Materialising a classification artifact here would duplicate a governed record owned elsewhere and risk it drifting out of step with the authoritative determination.

bundles.name: Invocation context and execution binding
bundles.description: Everything that was fixed at the moment of invocation: what was sent in, where it came from and how far it was trusted, which model and provider served the run, which decoding parameters applied, and which capability surface was exposed.
bundles.rationale: Reproducibility and audit both require the exact inputs and the exact bindings. OpenTelemetry deliberately makes content capture opt-in for privacy reasons while EU record-keeping pushes the other way, so the capture rule must be an explicit, recorded decision rather than an implementation accident.

layers.name: Request content and input trust
layers.description: The content actually presented to the model, how much of it is captured verbatim, and what is known about where each segment came from.

findings.name: Input messages, system instructions and payload handling
findings.description: What was sent to the model - system instructions, chat history, prompt variables and attachments - and under what capture rule. OpenTelemetry marks gen_ai.input.messages and gen_ai.system_instructions as opt-in with explicit sensitive-data warnings, and Bedrock externalises any body over 100 KB to object storage, so the run record must distinguish inline content from a reference plus digest.

questions.text: What exactly was presented to the model as system instructions, chat history, prompt variables and attachments?
Is verbatim input content captured, and under which opt-in, truncation, filtering or sampling rule was that decided?
Where content is too large or is binary, how is it externalised and referenced back from the run record?
How can the exact input be reconstructed later if the referenced payload store has since changed?
answer_data: Immutability guarantee of the payload store

data_elements.name: System instructions
data_elements.description: Instructions supplied outside the chat history that shaped model behaviour.

data_elements.name: Input messages
data_elements.description: Ordered chat history presented to the model for this run.

data_elements.name: Input payload reference
data_elements.description: Pointer to externally stored input content above the inline threshold.

data_elements.name: Input content digest
data_elements.description: Cryptographic digest binding the run record to the exact input bytes.

data_elements.name: Content capture mode
data_elements.description: Whether inputs are stored verbatim, truncated, redacted or omitted.

artifacts.name: Input payload object
artifacts.description: Externalised, immutable copy of the run's input content when it exceeds the inline threshold or is binary, referenced from the run record by URI and digest.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Content-addressed by digest, with the run identifier and role (system, message, attachment) recorded as metadata rather than as the name.

findings.name: Input segment provenance and trust level
findings.description: For each segment of the model's context, where it came from and how far it may be trusted. MCP states that tool annotations and tool results must be treated as untrusted unless the server is trusted, and directs clients to validate tool results before passing them to the model; a run record that flattens user text, retrieved documents and tool output into one undifferentiated context loses the evidence needed to investigate an injection.

questions.text: For each input segment, what is its origin - end user, retrieved document, tool result, upstream agent or system operator?
Which input segments were treated as untrusted data that must never be interpreted as instructions?
How is a suspected prompt-injection or untrusted-instruction attempt recorded against the run?

data_elements.name: Input segment origin
data_elements.description: Origin class of one delimited region of the model context.

data_elements.name: Input trust label
data_elements.description: Trust level assigned to an input segment at assembly time.

data_elements.name: Injection detection outcome
data_elements.description: Result of any untrusted-instruction detection applied to the context.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Trust labels are per-segment annotations over content already externalised as the input payload object; storing them as a separate artifact would duplicate segment boundaries and invite the two copies to disagree. They are therefore modelled as inline annotations carrying offsets into the referenced payload.

layers.name: Model, parameter and capability binding
layers.description: The exact execution substrate the run was bound to: model and provider, decoding parameters and configuration snapshot, and the tools and data sources made available.

findings.name: Model, provider and endpoint binding
findings.description: Which model was requested, which model actually answered, and through which provider, endpoint and region. OpenTelemetry keeps gen_ai.request.model and gen_ai.response.model separate precisely because a gateway or alias may resolve to a different model, and Bedrock records both a modelId and the serving region.

questions.text: Which model was requested and which model identifier actually produced the response?
Which provider, endpoint address and serving region handled the run?
Which model version, snapshot or inference profile is recorded so a later reader knows which weights answered?

data_elements.name: Requested model
data_elements.description: Model name or alias named in the request.

data_elements.name: Responding model
data_elements.description: Model that actually generated the response, which may differ from the request.

data_elements.name: Provider name
data_elements.description: Coded generative AI provider acting as telemetry-format discriminator.

data_elements.name: Server address
data_elements.description: Endpoint host serving the inference request.

data_elements.name: Serving region
data_elements.description: Geographic region or inference geography where the run executed.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Model and endpoint binding is a set of scalar attributes on the run record; the immutable artifact that describes what those identifiers mean - the versioned configuration and weight snapshot - is owned by the sibling configuration model and is referenced rather than copied, so that a single snapshot serves every run bound to it.

findings.name: Decoding parameters and reproducibility limits
findings.description: Which sampling and decoding parameters were in force and what actually prevents an identical re-execution. Anthropic marks temperature, top_p and top_k as deprecated for newer models, so a model that assumes these are always present and always determinative will mis-record reproducibility. The run references an immutable configuration snapshot rather than restating its content.

questions.text: Which sampling and decoding parameters were actually transmitted and honoured for this run?
answer_data: Temperature, top_p and top_k values where applicable

questions.text: Can this run be re-executed to produce an identical result, and what specifically prevents bit-identical reproduction?
How is a parameter recorded when the provider has deprecated, capped or silently ignored it for the selected model?
Which configuration snapshot does the run reference, and is that snapshot immutable and content-addressed?

data_elements.name: Maximum output tokens
data_elements.description: Upper bound on generated tokens requested for the run.

data_elements.name: Sampling parameters
data_elements.description: Temperature, top_p, top_k and related decoding controls as transmitted.

data_elements.name: Reproducibility class
data_elements.description: Whether the run is bit-reproducible, statistically reproducible or not reproducible.

data_elements.name: Configuration snapshot reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the immutable configuration the run was bound to.

data_elements.name: Configuration digest
data_elements.description: Digest proving which configuration content was in force.

artifacts.name: Configuration snapshot manifest
artifacts.description: Manifest listing the exact configuration content, parameters and digests the run was bound to, produced by the configuration model and referenced immutably by the run.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Content-addressed by digest of the canonicalised configuration; the run stores the reference and digest, never a mutable copy.

findings.name: Capability surface and granted scopes
findings.description: Which tools, resources and data sources the model could reach at each point in the run, and under which authorization scopes. MCP requires tool sets to be deterministic per authorization but permits them to change over time via list-changed notifications, and requires RFC 8707 resource indicators binding tokens to a specific server, so the surface is a time-varying, scope-bounded fact rather than a static list.

questions.text: Which tools, resources and data sources were offered to the model at run start, and in which order were they presented?
Which authorization scopes and resource indicators bounded what the run could reach?
Did the available capability set change during the run, and how is each change point recorded?
answer_data: Before and after tool set digests

data_elements.name: Tool catalogue snapshot reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the tool and resource list exposed to the run.

data_elements.name: Granted scopes
data_elements.description: Authorization scopes in force for the run's outbound calls.

data_elements.name: Resource indicator
data_elements.description: Canonical URI identifying the protected resource a token was issued for.

data_elements.name: Capability change event
data_elements.description: Recorded point where the available tool or resource set changed mid-run.

artifacts.name: Tool catalogue snapshot
artifacts.description: Frozen copy of the tool and resource definitions - names, titles, input and output schemas, annotations - as they were presented to the model during this run.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Content-addressed by digest of the canonicalised catalogue, with server canonical URI and capture instant as metadata.

bundles.name: Execution trajectory
bundles.description: What the run actually did, step by step: its internal decomposition and deliberation, its interactions with tools and retrieved data, and any work it delegated to sub-runs.
bundles.rationale: An agent run's accountability rests on the trajectory, not just the endpoints. OpenTelemetry models this as a span tree with plan, chat and execute_tool children, MCP defines the tool-call wire contract and explicitly tells clients to log tool usage for audit, and multi-agent delegation creates authority questions that only a recorded chain can answer.

layers.name: Step trajectory and deliberation
layers.description: How the run decomposes into ordered, nested steps, and how internal reasoning and planning output is treated.

findings.name: Step decomposition and deliberation capture
findings.description: The ordered, nested set of steps making up the run, and the treatment of intermediate reasoning. OpenTelemetry defines plan spans for task decomposition and counts inference_calls and tool_calls per agent invocation; Anthropic returns thinking blocks as first-class content. Reasoning content is high-sensitivity and often subject to a shorter retention rule than the final output, so its capture policy must be recorded rather than assumed.

questions.text: How is the run decomposed into ordered steps, and what identifies each step uniquely within the run?
What parent-child relationships hold between orchestration steps, model-call steps and tool-call steps?
Are intermediate reasoning or planning outputs captured, and under which disclosure and retention rule?
How many model calls and tool calls did the run make, and were any iteration limits reached?
answer_data: Iteration limit and whether it bound

data_elements.description: Identifier of one step within the run's trajectory.

data_elements.name: Step kind

data_elements.name: Parent step identifier

layers.name: Tool and environment interaction
layers.description: Calls the run made out to tools, servers and knowledge sources, and the evidence retained about each.

findings.name: Tool call record and effect character
findings.description: For each tool invocation: what was called, with what arguments, what came back, whether it failed, and what side-effect character the tool declared. MCP separates protocol errors (JSON-RPC error) from tool execution errors (isError true in the result) and warns that annotations are untrusted unless the server is trusted, so the record must keep the declaration and the trust judgement apart. Retries, timeouts and multi-round-trip input-required flows must be linked to one logical call.

questions.text: For each tool call, which tool on which server was invoked, with which arguments, and what did it return?
answer_data: Tool name and server canonical URI

questions.text: Did the call fail at protocol level or return an execution error, and how is that distinction preserved in the record?
What side-effect character did the tool declare - read-only, destructive, idempotent, open-world - and was that declaration treated as trusted?
How are retries, timeouts, cancellations and input-required round trips of the same logical call linked together?

data_elements.description: Identifier of a single tool invocation instance within the run.

data_elements.name: Tool name
data_elements.description: Name of the invoked tool, scoped to its serving server.

data_elements.name: Tool arguments
data_elements.description: Argument object supplied to the tool call.

data_elements.name: Tool result content
data_elements.description: Unstructured content blocks returned by the tool.

data_elements.name: Tool execution error flag
data_elements.description: Whether the tool reported an execution error in its result.

data_elements.name: Tool annotations
data_elements.description: Declared behaviour hints such as read-only, destructive or idempotent.

data_elements.name: Tool execution duration

artifacts.name: Tool call log entries
artifacts.description: Per-call audit entries capturing request, result, error disposition and timing for every tool invocation, satisfying the MCP guidance that clients log tool usage for audit purposes.

findings.name: Retrieval and grounding evidence
findings.description: Which knowledge sources were consulted and which retrieved items entered the model context. OpenTelemetry defines gen_ai.data_source.id for retrieval and grounding, but nothing normative pins the retrieved item to a resolvable version, so the run must record item references with digests and retrieval instants if the grounding is to be re-examined later.

questions.text: Which data sources or knowledge bases were queried to ground this run's output?
Which specific retrieved items entered the model context, and can each be re-resolved at the version that was used?
How fresh and how authoritative was the retrieved content at the instant it was used?

data_elements.name: Data source identifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of a knowledge base or corpus consulted during the run.

data_elements.name: Retrieved item reference
data_elements.description: Reference to one retrieved item placed into the model context.

data_elements.name: Retrieved item digest
data_elements.description: Digest fixing the exact version of a retrieved item.

data_elements.name: Retrieval instant
data_elements.description: Time at which the retrieval was performed.

artifacts.name: Retrieval evidence set
artifacts.description: The set of retrieved items, queries and relevance scores that grounded the run, retained so a reviewer can judge whether the output was supported by its sources.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Named by run identifier plus retrieval step identifier; each member item is content-addressed by its digest.

layers.name: Delegation and sub-runs
layers.description: Work this run handed to other agents or nested runs, and how authority, cost and outcome flow across the delegation boundary.

findings.name: Sub-run and multi-agent delegation
findings.description: Which sub-runs the run spawned, on whose authority each acted, and how their results roll up. OpenTelemetry provides invoke_workflow for coordinated multi-agent processes but defines no rollup semantics; PROV-O supplies actedOnBehalfOf for the responsibility chain. Unbounded recursion and authority widening across hops are the two failure modes the record has to make visible.

questions.text: Which sub-runs or delegated agent invocations did this run spawn, and in which order?
On whose authority did each sub-agent act, and was the granted authority narrowed at every delegation hop?
How are the cost, failure and output of a sub-run rolled up into the parent without double counting?
What terminates a delegation chain, and what prevents unbounded recursion or fan-out?

data_elements.name: Sub-run reference
data_elements.description: Reference to a run spawned by this run.

data_elements.name: Delegation depth
data_elements.description: Number of delegation hops between the originating run and this one.

data_elements.name: Delegated scope
data_elements.description: Authority actually conferred on a sub-agent for its sub-run.

data_elements.name: Rollup mode
data_elements.description: Rule by which sub-run measures are aggregated into the parent run.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Delegation is a typed edge between run records, not a document. Each sub-run is itself an instance of this model and owns its own artifacts; materialising a separate delegation artifact would create a third copy of facts already held on both endpoints and would go stale whenever a sub-run is corrected or redacted.

bundles.name: Outcome, state and time
bundles.description: How the run progressed through its states, why it ended, when everything happened, and what it produced.
bundles.rationale: Terminal state and termination reason drive downstream handling; EU AI Act Article 12(3) explicitly requires start and end date and time for each use of certain systems; and outputs need durable, digest-bound evidence plus, for media, a signed provenance manifest.

layers.name: Lifecycle state and temporal semantics
layers.description: The run's state machine, its termination outcome, and the time model that governs every instant recorded on it.

findings.name: Run state machine and termination outcome
findings.description: The legal states of a run and how it ended. OpenTelemetry records gen_ai.response.finish_reasons as an array and a Stable error.type when an operation ends in error; Anthropic returns stop_reason values end_turn, max_tokens and stop_sequence. A truncated run is neither a clean success nor a failure, and conflating the two destroys audit value.

questions.text: What is the complete set of run states, and which transitions between them are legal?
In which state did the run terminate, and for what stated reason?
How is a partially completed or truncated run distinguished from an outright failure for audit purposes?
Which low-cardinality error type is recorded when the run ends in error, and where does the full diagnostic live?

data_elements.name: Run status
data_elements.description: Current or terminal state of the run within its state machine.

data_elements.name: Finish or stop reason
data_elements.description: Reason generation terminated, such as natural end, token limit or stop sequence.

data_elements.name: Error type
data_elements.description: Low-cardinality classification of the error that ended the run.

data_elements.name: Completeness classification
data_elements.description: Whether the run completed fully, partially or not at all.

findings.inline_only_rationale: State and termination are coded scalar fields whose durable home is the run record artifact already declared under find-run-identifier. Emitting a separate state artifact would split the run's authoritative state across two objects and create an unresolvable question about which one wins after a correction.

findings.name: Temporal semantics and latency measures
findings.description: Every instant on the run, in a single governed format, with event time kept apart from observation, ingestion and billing-bucket time. RFC 3339 requires an explicit numeric offset or Z and reserves -00:00 for an unknown local offset. Anthropic's usage reporting is bucketed with a stated freshness lag, so cost timestamps are demonstrably not the same clock as execution timestamps.

questions.text: What are the run's start and end instants, and in which format and offset are they expressed?
How is the instant at which the run occurred distinguished from the instants at which it was observed, ingested and billed?
Which latency measures are recorded, and from whose vantage point are they measured?
answer_data: Time to first chunk or token

questions.text: Which clock source produced these instants, and what skew is tolerated before ordering becomes unreliable?

data_elements.name: Run start time
data_elements.description: Instant the run began, per the model timestamp rule.

data_elements.name: Run end time
data_elements.description: Instant the run reached a terminal state.

data_elements.name: Observation time
data_elements.description: Instant a telemetry collector observed the run event.

data_elements.name: Ingestion time
data_elements.description: Instant the record entered the durable store.

data_elements.name: Run duration
data_elements.description: Elapsed operation time in seconds.

data_elements.name: Time to first token
data_elements.description: Latency to the first streamed token or chunk.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Instants and durations are inline scalar values on the run and its step records, governed centrally by the model timestamp rule. A dedicated temporal artifact would either duplicate those scalars or become a second, competing source of truth about when the run happened.

layers.name: Outputs and generated assets
layers.description: What the run returned, how that return is evidenced, and what provenance travels with any media it produced.

findings.name: Output content, structure and evidence
findings.description: The content blocks the run produced, whether they validated against a declared schema, and how they are digested and referenced. MCP requires servers to make structured results conform to a declared outputSchema and clients to validate them; Bedrock externalises outputs above 100 KB. Which parts a human actually saw is a distinct and audit-relevant fact.

questions.text: Which content blocks did the run produce, in which modalities and in which order?
Was the output schema-constrained, and did it validate against the declared output schema?
How is the output stored, digested and referenced so a later reader can prove what was actually returned?
Which parts of the output were presented to a human, and which were consumed only by downstream machinery?

data_elements.name: Output messages
data_elements.description: Content blocks generated by the run, one set per candidate.

data_elements.name: Output payload reference
data_elements.description: Pointer to externally stored output content above the inline threshold.

data_elements.name: Output digest
data_elements.description: Digest binding the run record to the exact output bytes.

data_elements.name: Output schema reference
data_elements.description: Schema the structured output was required to satisfy.

data_elements.name: Output audience annotation
data_elements.description: Declared audience for a content block, such as user or assistant.

artifacts.name: Output payload object
artifacts.description: Externalised, immutable copy of the run's output content, referenced from the run record by URI and digest so the returned bytes remain provable after the run closes.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Content-addressed by digest; run identifier and candidate index are carried as metadata rather than embedded in the name.

findings.name: Generated asset provenance and AI disclosure
findings.description: For media assets the run produced, whether a signed content-provenance manifest is attached and what it asserts. C2PA 2.2 binds assertions and a claim through a claim signature with a hard binding to the content, and the c2pa.actions assertion carries a digitalSourceType disclosing generative-AI involvement. No normative C2PA field carries a run identifier, so the binding back to this model is an adopting-Dimension convention.

questions.text: For each media asset produced, is a signed provenance manifest attached, and which assertions does it carry?
Is the asset marked as AI-generated using a recognised digital source type, and does that marking survive downstream processing?
How is the manifest bound back to this run and to the ingredients that were consumed to create the asset?

data_elements.name: Provenance manifest reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the content-provenance manifest attached to a generated asset.

data_elements.name: Digital source type
data_elements.description: Coded disclosure of how the asset was produced, including AI generation.

data_elements.name: Ingredient references
data_elements.description: Assets consumed in producing the generated asset, carrying their own provenance.

data_elements.name: Hard binding hash
data_elements.description: Cryptographic hash binding the manifest to the asset bytes.

artifacts.name: Content provenance manifest
artifacts.description: Signed manifest of assertions, claim and claim signature travelling with a generated media asset, disclosing AI involvement and preserving the ingredient chain.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the manifest's own claim identifier and hard binding hash; the run identifier is recorded as a custom assertion because no normative C2PA field carries it.

bundles.name: Accountability, authority and provenance
bundles.description: Who authorised the run, who intervened in it, and to whom its activity, entities and effects are attributed.
bundles.rationale: An agent run acts with borrowed authority. MCP requires audience-bound tokens and forbids token passthrough; PROV-O supplies the vocabulary for attribution and delegation; EU AI Act Article 12(3) requires identifying the natural persons involved in verifying results for the most sensitive class. Without a recorded authority chain, effects cannot be traced to a responsible party.

layers.name: Actors, authority and oversight
layers.description: The principals behind the run, the scope they conferred, and the human decisions taken during execution.

findings.name: Principals, credentials and delegation of rights
findings.description: Which principal initiated the run and whose credentials were presented to each downstream resource. MCP requires tokens to be validated as issued specifically for the receiving server and forbids servers accepting or transiting foreign tokens; Bedrock records identity.arn for the calling principal. The record captures who and with what scope, never the credential material itself.

questions.text: Which principal initiated this run, and whose credentials were presented against each downstream resource?
Which scopes were granted, and was each access token bound to the specific resource it was used against?
Where the agent acted on behalf of a person or organisation, how is that on-behalf-of chain recorded?
How is an end user identified in the run record without persisting direct personal identifiers?

data_elements.name: Initiating principal
data_elements.description: Identity of the party whose action caused the run to start.

data_elements.name: Acted on behalf of
data_elements.description: Party on whose behalf the executing agent acted.

data_elements.name: Token audience
data_elements.description: Resource the presented access token was issued for.

data_elements.name: End user pseudonym
data_elements.description: Non-identifying reference to the end user associated with the run.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Authority facts are attributes and typed edges of the run record, and the underlying credential material must never be persisted anywhere in this model. Creating an authority artifact would produce an attractive target holding scope and audience data next to identifiers, with no offsetting audit benefit over the inline edges.

findings.name: Human oversight, approval and intervention
findings.description: Human decisions taken inside the run. MCP states there SHOULD always be a human able to deny tool invocations and that clients should show tool inputs before calling; EU AI Act Article 12(3)(d) requires identifying the natural persons involved in verifying results for Annex III point 1(a) systems. The record must capture what the decider was shown, not only what they decided.

questions.text: Which actions in this run required explicit human approval before they could execute?
Who approved or denied each gated action, at what instant, and what information were they shown at the time?
Was the run paused, stopped or overridden by a human, and what effect did that have on the trajectory?
How is a missing but required approval detected, escalated and recorded as a non-conformity?

data_elements.name: Approval request identifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of a human-approval request raised during the run.

data_elements.name: Approval decision
data_elements.description: Outcome of a human approval gate: approved, denied or timed out.

data_elements.name: Decider identity
data_elements.description: Identity of the natural person who approved, denied or verified.

data_elements.name: Presented context reference
data_elements.description: Reference to exactly what was shown to the human before deciding.

data_elements.name: Intervention type
data_elements.description: Kind of human intervention such as pause, stop, override or edit.

artifacts.name: Oversight decision record
artifacts.description: Evidence of each human approval, denial, verification or override during the run, including the decider, the instant and a reference to the exact information presented.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Named by run identifier plus approval request identifier; the decider is referenced by a governed person identifier held in the identity master system, not copied.

layers.name: Provenance and accountable party
layers.description: Formal provenance typing of the run and the identification of who owns the record and who answers for its effects.

findings.name: Provenance attribution, ownership and accountability
findings.description: How the run maps onto a formal provenance model and who is answerable. PROV-O types the run as an Activity with used and wasGeneratedBy edges to its inputs and outputs and wasAssociatedWith to its agent. Separately, EU AI Act Article 19 puts the log-keeping duty on the provider for logs under their control, which differs from the deployer who is answerable for effects, so record owner and accountable party are two distinct fields.

questions.text: Which provenance classes and properties does this run map to, and what are the resolvable IRIs for its activity and agents?
Who owns the run record, and who is the accountable deployer answerable for the run's effects?
Which outputs were derived from which inputs and retrieved items, and is that derivation edge explicit rather than inferred?
Under which tenant, workspace, project or cost centre is this run attributed?

data_elements.name: Provenance activity IRI
data_elements.description: Resolvable IRI typing the run as a provenance activity.

data_elements.name: Provenance agent IRI
data_elements.description: Resolvable IRI for an agent associated with the run.

data_elements.name: Derivation edges
data_elements.description: Explicit was-derived-from links between outputs and their sources.

data_elements.name: Record owner
data_elements.description: Party holding and controlling the run record.

data_elements.name: Accountable deployer
data_elements.description: Party answerable for the run's effects under the applicable regime.

data_elements.name: Tenant identifier
data_elements.description: Tenant, workspace or project the run is attributed to.

artifacts.name: Provenance graph fragment
artifacts.description: Graph projection of the run as a provenance activity with its used, generated, associated-with and acted-on-behalf-of edges, exportable for cross-system lineage queries.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Named by the activity IRI minted in the adopting Dimension's governed namespace, resolvable back to the run identifier.

bundles.name: Measurement, cost and quality evidence
bundles.description: What the run consumed, what it cost, how good its output was judged to be, and which policy checks it passed or failed.
bundles.rationale: The registry purpose names cost explicitly, and cost is the one dimension where no standard exists: OpenTelemetry's GenAI metrics define token usage and durations but no cost metric, while authoritative cost arrives later as a time-bucketed aggregate. Quality evidence is likewise a separate, often asynchronous event that must be bound back to the run.

layers.name: Consumption and cost
layers.description: Resource consumption attributable to the run and the monetary cost derived from it.

findings.name: Token and resource consumption
findings.description: What the run consumed. OpenTelemetry defines gen_ai.client.token.usage with token types input and output only, while providers report a richer set including cache-creation, cache-read and reasoning tokens, plus server-side tool use. Provider-reported counts and locally computed counts routinely disagree, so the reconciliation rule must be explicit.

questions.text: How many input, output, cache-read, cache-creation and reasoning tokens did the run consume?
Which non-token resources were consumed, and how is that set enumerated for this operation type?
How are provider-reported counts reconciled with locally computed counts when the two disagree?
Into which measurement time bucket is usage assigned when the run spans a bucket boundary?

data_elements.name: Input tokens
data_elements.description: Count of input tokens consumed, including cached tokens where reported.

data_elements.name: Output tokens
data_elements.description: Count of tokens generated by the run.

data_elements.name: Cache read tokens
data_elements.description: Input tokens served from a prompt cache.

data_elements.name: Cache creation tokens
data_elements.description: Input tokens written into a prompt cache for later reuse.

data_elements.name: Server tool use count
data_elements.description: Count of provider-side tool invocations such as web search.

data_elements.name: Usage counting authority
data_elements.description: Which party's count is treated as authoritative for this run.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Per-run consumption counters are scalar measures on the run record. The durable artifact in this area is the reconciled usage and cost statement declared on find-cost-attribution, which is produced later from authoritative bucketed reporting; duplicating counters into a second artifact here would guarantee divergence once reconciliation adjusts them.

findings.name: Cost attribution and reconciliation
findings.description: What the run cost and how confident that figure is. No GenAI telemetry standard defines a cost metric, and authoritative cost is published as daily aggregates in a single currency with a data-freshness lag and known exclusions such as priority-tier pricing. Per-run cost is therefore an estimate until reconciled, and the record must say which it is.

questions.text: What monetary cost is attributed to this run, in which currency and against which price basis?
Is the recorded cost a local estimate or an authoritative billed amount, and how is that status flagged and later upgraded?
To which API key, workspace, service tier and cost centre is this run's cost charged?
How are sub-run costs and cached-token savings allocated so that nothing is counted twice?

data_elements.name: Cost amount
data_elements.description: Monetary cost attributed to the run, in the smallest currency unit.

data_elements.name: Cost currency
data_elements.description: Currency in which the cost is expressed.

data_elements.name: Cost basis
data_elements.description: Whether the figure is a local estimate or an authoritative billed amount.

data_elements.name: Service tier
data_elements.description: Service tier under which the run was served, affecting pricing.

data_elements.name: API key identifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of the credential the usage is charged to, where applicable.

data_elements.name: Allocation method
data_elements.description: Rule for distributing shared and sub-run costs to this run.

artifacts.name: Usage and cost statement
artifacts.description: Reconciled statement joining the run's consumption counters to authoritative bucketed cost reporting, carrying the cost basis, reconciliation status and charge dimensions.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Named by run identifier plus the reporting bucket boundaries; superseded by a later statement rather than edited, with the supersession edge retained.

layers.name: Quality and safety evidence
layers.description: Evaluations, feedback and policy decisions that qualify how good and how safe this run was.

findings.name: Evaluation results and outcome quality
findings.description: Assessments bound to the run. OpenTelemetry defines gen_ai.evaluation.result as its own event, capable of being emitted independently of the trace, which means evaluation is frequently asynchronous and arrives after the run has closed. Human feedback is a distinct signal from automated evaluation and must not be merged into the same score field.

questions.text: Which evaluations were performed against this run's output, by which evaluator and at which evaluator version?
What score, label or verdict did each evaluation produce, and on what scale is it interpretable?
Was the evaluation performed inline during the run or asynchronously afterwards, and how late may it still arrive?
How is human feedback on the run captured and kept distinguishable from automated evaluation?

data_elements.name: Evaluation name
data_elements.description: Name of an evaluation applied to the run's output.

data_elements.name: Evaluator identifier
data_elements.description: Identity and version of the evaluating system or rubric.

data_elements.name: Evaluation score
data_elements.description: Numeric result produced by an evaluation.

data_elements.name: Evaluation label
data_elements.description: Categorical verdict produced by an evaluation.

data_elements.name: Feedback source
data_elements.description: Whether a quality signal came from a human or an automated evaluator.

artifacts.name: Evaluation result record
artifacts.description: Standalone record of one evaluation applied to the run, emitted independently of the trace and referencing the run by identifier.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Named by evaluation identifier assigned by the evaluating system, with the run identifier and evaluator version carried as references.

findings.name: Guardrail and policy decisions
findings.description: Policy checks applied to inputs and outputs, their verdicts, and the policy version in force. A blocked or refused run creates a genuine tension: the record must prove the block occurred without persisting the prohibited content, so the model records decision metadata and digests rather than the content itself.

questions.text: Which policy or guardrail checks were applied to this run's inputs, intermediate steps and outputs?
What did each check decide - allow, transform or block - and what exactly was modified?
Which policy version was in force at the instant of each decision?
How is a blocked or refused run evidenced without persisting the prohibited content itself?

data_elements.name: Guardrail name
data_elements.description: Name of a policy or safety check applied during the run.

data_elements.name: Guardrail version
data_elements.description: Version of the policy in force when the decision was made.

data_elements.name: Guardrail decision
data_elements.description: Verdict returned by a guardrail: allow, transform or block.

data_elements.name: Refusal code
data_elements.description: Coded reason a run or step was refused, recorded without the content.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Guardrail outcomes are decision annotations attached to the run and its steps. Deliberately, the prohibited or transformed content is not persisted, so there is no payload to externalise; producing an artifact here would either be empty metadata duplicated from the run record or would reintroduce the very content the block existed to prevent retaining.

bundles.name: Governance of the run record
bundles.description: How the record of the run is retained, protected, exposed and exported once the run itself is over.
bundles.rationale: The run ends in seconds; the record lives for years. EU AI Act Article 19 sets a minimum retention of at least six months for provider-held logs, content-capture attributes carry explicit sensitive-data warnings, and no cross-vendor run schema exists, so retention, access, integrity and export all need governed answers.

layers.name: Retention and record integrity
layers.description: How long the record is kept, under what basis, how it is disposed of, and how alteration is made detectable.

findings.name: Statutory log content, retention and disposal
findings.description: The regulated content and lifespan of the record. Article 19 requires providers to keep automatically generated logs under their control for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and at least six months unless other Union or national law provides otherwise, with financial institutions keeping them under sectoral rules. That floor collides with data-minimisation and erasure duties, so the reconciliation rule must be recorded rather than left to the operator.

questions.text: Which regulated minimum log elements must this run's record contain, and is each one demonstrably present?
For how long must the record be kept, counted from which start point, and on which legal basis?
Who holds the logs when provider and deployer differ, and how is the phrase under their control demonstrated?
How are erasure requests, legal holds and statutory minimum-retention duties reconciled when they conflict?
What exactly is destroyed at end of life, and what tombstone remains to prove the record once existed?

data_elements.name: Retention class
data_elements.description: Coded retention rule governing this run record.

data_elements.name: Retention until
data_elements.description: Earliest instant at which the record may lawfully be disposed of.

data_elements.name: Legal basis
data_elements.description: Cited basis for retaining or erasing the record.

data_elements.name: Legal hold flag
data_elements.description: Whether disposal is suspended by an active hold.

data_elements.name: Disposition action
data_elements.description: Action taken at end of retention: destroy, redact or transfer.

data_elements.name: Tombstone reference
data_elements.description: Minimal residue proving a disposed record previously existed.

artifacts.name: Retention and hold register
artifacts.description: Register recording the retention class, computed disposal date, active holds, erasure requests and disposition outcomes for run records, enabling proof of both retention and lawful destruction.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Register entries are named by run identifier plus retention-decision ordinal; the register itself is identified by its governing retention schedule reference.

findings.name: Record integrity and tamper evidence
findings.description: How a closed run record is made alteration-evident. C2PA demonstrates the pattern that matters here: assertions gathered into a claim, hashed, and covered by a claim signature verifiable against a trust anchor. A run record without a seal cannot support an accountability claim, and corrections must be recorded as new assertions rather than overwrites.

questions.text: How is the run record sealed at close so that any later alteration becomes detectable?
Which fields become immutable when the run closes, and which may still legitimately be appended afterwards?
How is a correction recorded without overwriting the original assertion?
Who can verify the seal, against which trust anchor, and what happens when verification fails?

data_elements.name: Record digest
data_elements.description: Digest over the canonicalised run record at seal time.

data_elements.name: Digest algorithm
data_elements.description: Algorithm used to compute the record digest.

data_elements.name: Seal signature
data_elements.description: Signature covering the record digest and its metadata.

data_elements.name: Sealed at
data_elements.description: Instant at which the record was sealed.

data_elements.name: Correction of
data_elements.description: Reference from a correcting record to the assertion it supersedes.

artifacts.name: Integrity seal
artifacts.description: Signed digest covering the closed run record and its referenced payload digests, giving an independent verifier the means to detect any later alteration.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the record digest it covers, with the run identifier, signer identity and seal instant carried as metadata.

layers.name: Access control and interoperability
layers.description: Who may see which parts of the record, and how the record moves into and out of external schemas.

findings.name: Access scoping and confidentiality of run content
findings.description: Separating access to run metadata from access to run content. OpenTelemetry warns explicitly that input messages, output messages, system instructions, prompt variables and tool definitions are likely to contain sensitive and personal data, which makes field-level rather than record-level access control the default position. Residency constraints on the record may differ from those on the inference itself.

questions.text: Who may read run inputs and outputs, as opposed to run metadata and measures only?
Which fields are classified as sensitive, and what masking or truncation applies by default?
Which accesses to the run record must themselves be logged, and what does that access log capture?
Which residency or cross-border constraints bind the record, and how do they differ from the constraints on the inference itself?

data_elements.name: Sensitivity classification
data_elements.description: Confidentiality class assigned to a field or payload of the run.

data_elements.name: Field-level access rule
data_elements.description: Rule granting or denying a role access to a specific field set.

data_elements.name: Record residency region
data_elements.description: Region in which the run record must be stored.

data_elements.name: Masking rule
data_elements.description: Default transformation applied to sensitive content on read.

artifacts.name: Access audit trail
artifacts.description: Append-only trail of reads, exports and unmasking events against run records, capturing who accessed which fields, when and under what authorisation.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Entries are named by run identifier plus a zero-padded, gapless access ordinal; the accessing principal is referenced by governed identity, never copied.

findings.name: Export profiles and schema mapping
findings.description: Projecting the run into external schemas and importing foreign run records without silently mis-stating their origin. Because gen_ai.* attributes are still in Development status, and providers differ in identifiers and usage fields, every mapping is provisional and lossy in known ways; the model records the loss rather than claiming conformance.

questions.text: Into which external schemas can a run record be projected, and which profile governs each projection?
Which fields have no target in a given external schema, and how is that loss declared to the consumer?
How are vendor-specific attributes carried without polluting the canonical model?
How is an imported third-party run record marked as externally asserted rather than locally observed?

data_elements.name: Export profile identifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of the governed profile controlling one projection.

data_elements.name: Target schema URI
data_elements.description: Versioned URI of the external schema a projection targets.

data_elements.name: Unmapped fields
data_elements.description: Canonical fields with no counterpart in the target schema.

data_elements.name: Extension namespace
data_elements.description: Namespace carrying vendor-specific attributes outside the canonical set.

data_elements.name: Assertion origin
data_elements.description: Whether a record was locally observed or externally asserted and imported.

artifacts.name: Run export package
artifacts.description: Self-contained projection of one run into a named external profile, bundling the mapped record, the field mapping table and an explicit declaration of unmapped fields.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Named by run identifier plus export profile identifier and profile version; regenerated rather than edited when the profile changes.

functions.name: Open run
functions.description: Accept an invocation, assign the authoritative run identifier, bind the run to a configuration snapshot, capability surface and principal, and record the start instant.
inputs: Invocation request with operation type and inputs
Correlation context (traceparent, conversation identifier, parent run)
outputs: Run record in active state with authoritative identifier
Recorded start instant and correlation keys
Capability surface snapshot reference
preconditions: The configuration snapshot is immutable and resolvable by digest
The presented token is audience-bound to each intended resource
The applicable content-capture mode has been determined for this run class
effects: Run enters the active state and becomes referenceable by other records
Start event time is fixed and cannot later be edited
Retention clock start point is established

functions.name: Record step
functions.description: Append one ordered step to the run trajectory: a planning step, a model call, a tool call or a delegated sub-run reference, with its payload references, timings and error disposition.
inputs: Run identifier and parent step reference
Step kind and payload or payload reference
outputs: Appended step record with gapless sequence index
Updated inference-call and tool-call counters
preconditions: The run is in an active state
Payloads above the inline threshold have been externalised and digested

Protocol errors and tool execution errors are kept distinguishable

The decider can be shown the actual arguments before the call is made

Decider identity and presented context become part of the audit evidence

Completeness classification and end instant
Provisional cost figure flagged as an estimate

The run is not already in a terminal state

Late-arriving evaluations and reconciled costs may still be appended within the declared window
